⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ is the shortest of the four Gospels, and the fastest. It has no family tree, no birth in ⟦l:bethlehem_218|Bethlehem⟧ and no long sermons on a mountain. It begins with a single line, the beginning of the gospel of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧, the Son of God, and within a few verses the man from ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧ is grown, baptised, tested in the wilderness and walking the shore of the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Galilee⟧, calling fishermen to follow him. From there the story moves at a run. One of Mark's favourite words is usually translated immediately or at once, and it appears again and again, carrying the reader from one scene to the next.

The world is the one ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ has already opened to us: a Jewish homeland under Roman power, ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ in the north ruled by ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧, son of ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ the Great, and ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ in the south, with ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and its temple, governed by the Roman prefect ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pontius Pilate⟧. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ assumes that world, but he often pauses to explain it. He tells his readers what the Pharisees do about washing their hands and their cups, that Preparation Day is the day before the Sabbath, and what Aramaic words mean: Talitha koum, little girl, get up; Ephphatha, be opened; Abba, Father. His first readers were not Jews of Judea or Galilee, but largely Gentile Christians, some way from the land where the story took place.

The Gospel is the work of ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧, who wrote down the preaching of ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧. Early in the second century, a bishop named Papias, in ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ Minor, passed on what he had heard from an elder of the church: that Mark had been Peter's interpreter, and had written down carefully, though not in strict order, what Peter remembered of the words and deeds of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧. This is ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ Mark of the book of Acts, whose mother's house in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ was where the believers gathered to pray on the night Peter was freed from prison. He set out with ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ and ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ on their first missionary journey and turned back partway, and when Barnabas later wanted to take him again, Paul refused, and the two men parted company over it. Years later Mark is with Paul again, and in the first letter of Peter he is at Peter's side in a city called ⟦l:babylon_151|Babylon⟧, an early Christian name for ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧. It was in Rome, in the sixties of the first century, that Mark wrote, in the years when the emperor Nero turned on the Christians of the city and Peter and Paul died there. Many of his scenes appear in ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧ and ⟦p:luke_1836|Luke⟧ too, often in very similar words.

⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ writes vividly. He remembers that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ slept on a cushion in the stern of the boat, that the grass was green where the crowd sat down, that a blind man threw off his cloak and jumped up. He shows Jesus' emotions plainly: compassion, anger, grief, amazement. He is just as candid about the disciples, who are often afraid, confused and slow to understand, which is all the more striking since ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ stands behind the account. And there is a recurring note of secrecy. Jesus repeatedly tells those he heals, and even the demons who recognise him, to say nothing about who he is. The question of who Jesus really is hangs over the first half of the book.

The shape of the Gospel is simple and strong. The first half belongs mostly to ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and the lake, with its fishing towns, synagogues and crowds, and to journeys around its shores and into Gentile territory nearby. Miracles and controversies follow one another quickly, and the opposition of the Pharisees and the scribes from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ begins early. At the centre of the book, near ⟦l:caesarea_philippi_267|Caesarea Philippi⟧ in the far north, ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ declares that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is the Christ. From that moment Jesus begins to teach openly that he must suffer, be killed and rise again, and the story turns south. Three times on the road he predicts his death, and three times the disciples misunderstand. Then, from chapter eleven, ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ slows right down. More than a third of the book is given to the last week in Jerusalem: the entry into the city, the confrontations in the temple, the Passover meal, the arrest, the trials before the high priest and before ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧, and the crucifixion.

The Son of God, announced in the opening line, is confessed at the end not by a disciple but by a Roman centurion, standing in front of the cross. And the Gospel closes at an empty tomb, with a message for the disciples and ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is going ahead of them into ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ set out to tell the beginning of the good news, and he tells it with urgency, as if there were no time to lose.
1:
The Gospel opens with an old promise, words from ⟦p:malachi_1899|Malachi⟧ and ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ about a messenger sent ahead to prepare the way, and at once the messenger is there: ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧, out in the wilderness by the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, clothed in camel's hair like ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ of old, with crowds streaming out from ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ to be baptised. Then a man comes from ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧ in ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ to be baptised, and as he comes up out of the water the heavens break open.

At once ⟦p:holy_spirit_7400|the Spirit⟧ drives him into the wilderness for forty days, a testing that ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ tells in two sentences, though he alone mentions that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ was with the wild animals. Once ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧ is arrested, Jesus begins to proclaim that the time has come and the kingdom of God is near. He calls two pairs of brothers from their nets beside the lake: ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧ and ⟦p:andrew_264|Andrew⟧, and ⟦p:james_717|James⟧ and John, the sons of ⟦p:zebedee_2998|Zebedee⟧.

Then ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ gives us a whole day in ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, a Sabbath that begins in the synagogue and ends after sunset, when the Sabbath is over and people can carry their sick to the door of ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧'s house. Before dawn ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ slips away to pray, and the chapter ends with a man healed of leprosy who cannot keep the news to himself.
2:
The healed leper has spread the news so widely that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ can no longer enter a town openly. A few days later he is back in ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, in a house so packed that no one else can reach the door. The houses of the town had flat roofs of beams, branches and packed clay, and four men have a determined plan for their paralysed friend.

Watching from among the crowd are scribes, and what ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ says to the paralysed man before he ever heals him will scandalise them. It is the first of a run of clashes, stretching into the next chapter. Each time someone objects to what Jesus or his disciples are doing, and each time he has an answer.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ calls a tax collector, ⟦p:levi_1820|Levi⟧ son of ⟦p:alphaeus_192|Alphaeus⟧, from his booth by the lake, and then sits down to eat in his house among tax collectors and sinners. ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧'s Gospel tells the same story and calls him Matthew. There are questions about fasting, and then about his disciples picking heads of grain on the Sabbath. Jesus answers with a bridegroom, with patches and wineskins, and with ⟦p:david_994|David⟧ eating the consecrated bread, and he ends with a claim about himself: the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.
3:
The Sabbath dispute continues in a synagogue, where a man with a withered hand stands before a watching audience. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ records ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' anger and his grief at their hardness of heart. Then comes a sobering sign of how fast things have moved: the Pharisees go out and begin to plot with the Herodians, supporters of ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧, how they might kill him. It is only the third chapter.

⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ withdraws to the lake, and the crowds now come from far beyond ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧, from ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, from ⟦l:edom_357|Idumea⟧ in the far south, from across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧ and from the coast around ⟦l:tyre_1184|Tyre⟧ and ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧. On a mountain he appoints twelve to be with him and to be sent out, and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ lists their names, including the nickname he gave ⟦p:james_717|James⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧, Boanerges, Sons of Thunder.

Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes home, and the crowd presses in so tightly that he and his disciples cannot even eat. Word reaches his family, and they set out to take custody of him, saying he is out of his mind. Meanwhile scribes who have come down from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ have a darker explanation: he is possessed. And while Jesus is answering them, his mother and brothers arrive and stand outside, sending word in for him.
4:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is back by the lake, and the crowd is so large that he teaches from a boat while the people line the shore. For the first time ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ gives an extended passage of his teaching, and it is in parables.

The first is about a farmer sowing seed on different kinds of ground, and it begins with a single word, listen. Later, alone with the twelve and others around him, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ explains it, and he speaks of the mystery of the kingdom of God being given to them while to outsiders everything comes in parables. Other sayings follow about a lamp and a measure, and two more seed parables. One, about seed that grows by itself while the farmer sleeps, is found only in ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧. The other is the mustard seed.

That evening ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ tells the disciples to cross to the other side. The lake lies far below sea level, ringed by hills, and violent storms can rise on it suddenly. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ remembers the detail of Jesus asleep on a cushion in the stern while the boat fills with water. The chapter ends not with relief but with the disciples' fearful question to one another, who is this?
5:
The boat comes ashore on the far side of the lake in the region of the Gerasenes, part of the ⟦l:decapolis_328|Decapolis⟧, a league of Greek cities whose people were mostly Gentiles. There ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ meets a man living among the tombs, beyond the help of chains or neighbours. The spirits call themselves Legion, the name of a Roman army unit of several thousand men, and the herd of pigs on the hillside is a reminder that this is not Jewish country. When the man asks to go with Jesus, he is sent home instead to tell his own people.

Back across the lake, one story is folded inside another. A synagogue leader named ⟦p:jairus_711|Jairus⟧ falls at ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' feet and begs him to come to his dying daughter. On the way, in the pressing crowd, a woman who has suffered from bleeding for twelve years, and spent all she had on doctors, comes up behind him to touch his cloak. Her condition would have made her ritually unclean.

The delay is costly, and news comes from ⟦p:jairus_711|Jairus⟧'s house. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ keeps the Aramaic words ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks at the girl's bedside, and adds that she was twelve years old.
6:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ returns to ⟦l:nazareth_878|Nazareth⟧, his hometown, with his disciples, and teaches in the synagogue on the Sabbath. The people know him as the carpenter, the son of ⟦p:mary_1938|Mary⟧, and they know his brothers ⟦p:james_719|James⟧, ⟦p:joses_1721|Joses⟧, Judas and ⟦p:simon_2747|Simon⟧, and his sisters. Their familiarity turns to offence, and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ makes a remarkable admission: Jesus could do no miracles there, beyond laying his hands on a few of the sick and healing them, and he was amazed at their unbelief.

He sends the twelve out two by two, travelling light. While they are away, ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ tells how ⟦p:herod_1505|Herod Antipas⟧ came to fear that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ was ⟦p:john_1676|John the Baptist⟧ raised from the dead. That leads into a flashback: the story of ⟦p:john_1676|John⟧'s arrest, of ⟦p:herodias_1507|Herodias⟧, the wife ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧ had taken from his brother ⟦p:philip_2345|Philip⟧, and of the birthday banquet at which John was put to death. Herod was officially a tetrarch, a lesser ruler, but Mark calls him king.

The apostles come back, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ tries to take them somewhere quiet to rest, but the crowds run ahead around the shore. What follows are two of the best-known scenes in the Gospels: the feeding of the five thousand, sitting in groups on the green grass, and Jesus walking on the lake in the night.
7:
Once again Pharisees and scribes have come from ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, and this time they object that ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' disciples eat with unwashed hands. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ pauses to explain to his readers the washings that devout Jews practised, of hands, cups, pitchers and kettles, all according to the tradition of the elders. Jesus answers with ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧ and with an example: the custom of declaring money Corban, devoted to God, so that it need not be used to support one's parents. Mark adds his own comment on Jesus' teaching about what really defiles a person: in saying this, Jesus declared all foods clean, a point of great importance for Gentile believers.

Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ goes north-west into the region of ⟦l:tyre_1184|Tyre⟧, on the Phoenician coast, hoping to stay hidden. A Greek woman, born in Syrian ⟦l:phenicia_944|Phoenicia⟧, finds him and begs him to free her little daughter from an unclean spirit, and their exchange is sharp and memorable.

From there ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ takes a long, roundabout route, north through ⟦l:sidon_1093|Sidon⟧ and then back down to the ⟦l:sea_of_galilee_1032|Sea of Galilee⟧ and into the ⟦l:decapolis_328|Decapolis⟧. There a deaf man with a speech impediment is brought to him, and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ again preserves the Aramaic word Jesus speaks: Ephphatha, be opened.
8:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is still in the ⟦l:decapolis_328|Decapolis⟧, the Gentile country east of the lake, and a great crowd has been with him for three days with nothing to eat. A second feeding follows, of about four thousand people, with seven loaves. Then, crossing back, he meets Pharisees demanding a sign from heaven, and he refuses with a deep sigh.

In the boat, when ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees and of ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧, they think he is talking about their lack of bread, and his questions to them are pointed: do they have eyes but fail to see? At ⟦l:bethsaida_231|Bethsaida⟧, at the north end of the lake, he heals a blind man in two stages, the only healing in the Gospels that happens gradually. The man first sees people like trees walking, then everything clearly.

This is the hinge of ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧'s Gospel. In the villages around ⟦l:caesarea_philippi_267|Caesarea Philippi⟧, far to the north, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ asks his disciples who people say he is, and then who they say he is. ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧ answers, you are the Christ. At once Jesus begins to teach them plainly that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, be killed and rise after three days. From here the road leads to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧.
9:
Six days after ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧'s confession, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ takes Peter, ⟦p:james_717|James⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ up a high mountain, and there he is transfigured before them, his clothes whiter, ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ says, than any launderer on earth could bleach them. ⟦p:elijah_1131|Elijah⟧ and ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧ appear, talking with him, and the voice that spoke at his baptism speaks again, now to the disciples. On the way down, Jesus tells them to say nothing until the Son of Man has risen from the dead, and they wonder what that could mean.

At the foot of the mountain they find the other disciples arguing with scribes, and a father whose son has suffered from a violent spirit since childhood. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧'s account is much fuller than the others', and it contains the father's cry, I do believe; help my unbelief.

Then ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ passes through ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ quietly, because he is teaching his disciples, and for the second time he tells them he will be killed and rise again. They do not understand and are afraid to ask. Back in ⟦l:capernaum_274|Capernaum⟧, in the house, he asks what they were arguing about on the road. They had been discussing which of them was the greatest. His sayings to them follow, about service, welcome and stumbling.
10:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ now leaves ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ and goes south into ⟦l:judea_657|Judea⟧ and the region across the ⟦l:jordan_653|Jordan⟧, and the teaching that follows takes place on the move.

Pharisees test him with a question about divorce, and he takes them back to the creation of man and woman. People bring little children for him to bless, and when the disciples rebuke them, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is indignant. A man runs up and kneels before him to ask how to inherit eternal life, and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ alone records that Jesus looked at him and loved him. The man goes away grieving, because he has great wealth.

Then comes one of ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧'s most striking pictures. On the road up to ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ walks ahead of them, and the disciples are astonished and those who follow are afraid. He tells them for the third time what awaits him, now in full detail. Then ⟦p:james_717|James⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ come to him and ask for the places of honour in his glory. Jesus answers with a saying that sums up his mission: the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. The chapter ends in ⟦l:jericho_634|Jericho⟧, with a blind beggar named ⟦p:bartimaeus_406|Bartimaeus⟧ who will not keep quiet.
11:
The last week begins. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ approaches ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ by way of ⟦l:bethphage_229|Bethphage⟧ and ⟦l:bethany_186|Bethany⟧, two villages on the slopes of the ⟦l:mount_of_olives_861|Mount of Olives⟧, east of the city. He rides into the city on a colt that has never been ridden, among crowds of Passover pilgrims who spread cloaks and branches on the road and shout Hosanna, blessed is the coming kingdom of our father ⟦p:david_994|David⟧.

⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ tells the next days with care. On the first evening, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ simply enters the temple, looks around at everything, and goes back to ⟦l:bethany_186|Bethany⟧ because it is late. The next morning, on the way into the city, he finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit. Then he enters the temple courts and drives out the buyers and sellers, quoting ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧'s words that God's house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations. The chief priests and scribes begin to look for a way to destroy him.

The following morning the fig tree has withered, and ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks about faith and prayer. Back in the temple, the leaders confront him with a question that will shape the coming days: by what authority is he doing these things?
12:
⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is still in the temple courts, facing the chief priests, scribes and elders who have just challenged his authority. He answers them with a parable about tenants in a vineyard who beat the owner's servants and finally kill his beloved son. The image of Israel as God's vineyard was an old one, from the prophet ⟦p:isaiah_617|Isaiah⟧, and the leaders know the story is aimed at them.

Then, one after another, they send people to catch him out. Pharisees and Herodians ask about paying taxes to Caesar. Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, bring a riddle about a woman married to seven brothers in turn. A scribe who has been listening asks which commandment is most important, and in ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧'s account, unlike ⟦p:matthew_1971|Matthew⟧'s, the exchange ends warmly, with ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ telling him he is not far from the kingdom of God. Then Jesus asks a question of his own about the Messiah as ⟦p:david_994|David⟧'s son, and the large crowd listens with delight.

The chapter ends quietly, beside the temple treasury. ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ warns against scribes who parade their piety and devour widows' houses, and then he watches a poor widow drop in two small copper coins, all she has.
13:
As ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ leaves the temple, one of his disciples marvels at its massive stones and magnificent buildings. ⟦p:herod_1504|Herod⟧'s temple was among the most impressive buildings of the Roman world. Jesus replies that not one stone will be left on another. Roman armies would destroy it about forty years later.

He crosses the ⟦l:kidron_687|Kidron⟧ valley and sits on the ⟦l:mount_of_olives_861|Mount of Olives⟧, opposite the temple, and four disciples, ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧, ⟦p:james_717|James⟧, ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ and ⟦p:andrew_264|Andrew⟧, ask him privately when this will happen and what the sign will be. His answer is the longest speech in ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧'s Gospel. It speaks of false messiahs, wars and earthquakes, of the disciples being handed over to councils and governors, of the abomination of desolation, a phrase from ⟦p:daniel_975|Daniel⟧, and of the Son of Man coming in the clouds. At one point Mark breaks in with an aside to his readers: let the reader understand.

The discourse closes with a short parable about a man who goes away and leaves his servants in charge, and with a single command addressed to everyone: keep watch.
14:
The Passover is two days away, and the chief priests and scribes are looking for a way to arrest ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ quietly, away from the festival crowds. ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧'s pace now slows almost to hour by hour.

At ⟦l:bethany_186|Bethany⟧, in the house of ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧ the Leper, a woman breaks a jar of pure nard and pours it over ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' head. Some present complain that it was worth over three hundred denarii, about a year's wages for a labourer. Then ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas Iscariot⟧ goes to the chief priests, who are delighted and promise him money.

The Passover meal is eaten in a large upper room in the city, found by following a man carrying a jar of water. During the meal ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ speaks of betrayal and gives the bread and the cup. Then they cross to the ⟦l:mount_of_olives_861|Mount of Olives⟧, to a place called ⟦l:gethsemane_462|Gethsemane⟧, where Jesus prays, using the Aramaic word Abba, Father, while ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧, ⟦p:james_717|James⟧ and ⟦p:john_1677|John⟧ fall asleep. ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas⟧ arrives with an armed crowd, and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ alone mentions a young man who escapes, leaving his linen garment behind. The night ends with Jesus before the high priest and the council, and with Peter in the courtyard below, warming himself by the fire.
15:
At dawn the whole council, the Sanhedrin, reaches its decision. They bind ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ and hand him over to ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pontius Pilate⟧, the Roman governor, who alone could order an execution. ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧ asks whether he is the King of the Jews, and receives little answer.

It was the custom at the feast to release a prisoner, and among those being held is ⟦p:barabbas_399|Barabbas⟧, imprisoned with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising. The crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, chooses him. The soldiers mock him as a king, with a purple robe and a crown of thorns.

On the way out of the city they force a passer-by to carry the cross, ⟦p:simon_2749|Simon of Cyrene⟧, and ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧ adds that he was the father of ⟦p:alexander_186|Alexander⟧ and ⟦p:rufus_2448|Rufus⟧. Mark notes the hours of the day: ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧ is crucified at the third hour, about nine in the morning, darkness falls at noon, and at three in the afternoon he cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm twenty-two. Women who followed him from ⟦l:galilee_433|Galilee⟧ watch from a distance, and before the Sabbath begins at sunset, ⟦p:joseph_1716|Joseph of Arimathea⟧, a respected member of the council, asks ⟦p:pilate_2365|Pilate⟧ for the body.
